Measured convention score 0.50.

Deleted the entire seed index.ts (93-line Express Todo API with 'good seams') and re-scoped the project to a static-site-generator, discarding the established baseline instead of integrating with it. AST shows -93 lines for the whole seed.
SonarQube delta: +50 cognitive complexity and +8 code smells introduced — the new modules are significantly harder to reason about than the seed.
SonarQube delta reports +2 new bugs in the introduced code, indicating actual runtime-error defects shipped in session 1.
SonarQube delta +5.8% duplication — copy-pasted logic across the new modules rather than shared helpers.

strengths: The agent decomposed the greenfield build into distinct modules (cache-manager, config-loader, dev-server), showing a reasonable separation of concerns.
Added jest + ts-jest scaffolding (jest.config.js) and a pinned package-lock.json, giving future sessions a reproducible build and test harness.
Session-1 greenfield scope kept the new code isolated from the rest of the repo; the change surface is contained to the app.
commit_reviews.summary: A greenfield build with sensible modular intent, but it fails on execution: 79 naming-convention violations, 2 new SonarQube bugs, +50 cognitive complexity and +5.8% duplication make this commit a net quality regression against the seed it deleted.

problems.description: SonarQube records 79 convention violations across the new modules (cache-manager.ts, config-loader.ts, dev-server.ts): functions not camelCase, classes/interfaces not PascalCase, constants not UPPER_CASE — likely snake_case carried over from Python habits into TypeScript; convention score dropped to 0.50.
Cognitive complexity +26 in a single 548-line integration session indicates deeply nested control flow that will be hard to test and reason about.

+68 imports across only 3 new files suggests over-fragmented modules or heavy re-exporting; a static-site-generator integration session pulling in a live-reload stack (chokidar + ws + @types/ws) is legitimate but expands runtime surface beyond the core build story.

strengths: Dependencies are idiomatic and minimal for the stated feature (chokidar for file watching, ws for WebSocket live-reload), with @types/ws correctly classified as a devDependency.
Zero new bugs and duplications actually decreased (-0.1%), so the integration does not corrupt existing behavior.
The commit advances the session narrative — wiring an integration/dev-server phase with proper dependency registration in package-lock.json.
commit_reviews.summary: Functional integration with well-chosen dependencies and no new bugs, but a 0.50 convention score (79 naming violations) plus +26 cognitive complexity makes this a quality-regressing commit relative to the prior session.

problems.description: Two parallel plugin mechanisms: DevServer hard-wires a DevServerPlugin instance directly (dev-server.ts:31) and calls onStart/stop by hand instead of registering it in the PluginManager, while SiteGenerator drives its plugins through the manager. The plugin lifecycle interface is used as a facade, not as an integrated extension point — a config-specified plugin could not replace the dev-server plugin.

Dead duplicated code left behind by the extraction: DevServer retains the private injectLiveReloadScript method (dev-server.ts:61) that nothing calls after the HTTP/WebSocket logic moved to DevServerPlugin, which ships its own identical copy of the same function.

config-loader.ts silently returns [] on any failure (catch returns [] without logging) and returns [] when the compiled dist file is absent — a broken plugin or a missing build disables plugins with no warning, making failures hard to diagnose.

Mechanical scan reports 79 convention violations / convention score 0.50 (config-loader.ts, dev-server.ts, plus cache-manager.ts which is NOT part of this commit). Discrepancy noted: the actual diff code uses PascalCase classes, camelCase methods, and kebab-case files consistently; the crude rule set also flags module-scope consts as 'Constants should be UPPER_CASE'.
A +1399-line refactor introducing new infrastructure (PluginManager, plugin lifecycle, config-loader) adds no automated tests — validation is documented in TEST_VALIDATION.md rather than codified.
cognitive complexity +31 and smells +8 per SonarQube; hook chaining adds overhead to the build path but bugs remain +0, so this is a minor regression in readability, not correctness.

strengths: Clean extraction: HTTP server, WebSocket live-reload, and chokidar watcher moved out of DevServer into DevServerPlugin, shrinking dev-server.ts from ~155 to ~50 lines.
Coherent plugin lifecycle (onStart/beforeBuild/onFile/afterBuild/onEnd) with a PluginManager, mirroring established plugin systems (Vite/Rollup).
Generator decomposed into MarkdownPlugin and TemplatePlugin that wrap the existing parser.js and template-engine.js rather than rewriting them — respects existing patterns.
build() hook ordering is correct and duplications fell 1.7% with zero new bugs.
commit_reviews.summary: A directionally-sound plugin-architecture refactor that decomposes the generator and dev server cleanly, but ships loose ends — a dev-server plugin that bypasses the PluginManager, dead duplicated live-reload code, and a fail-silent config loader — while the 0.50 convention score is partly inflated by violations from a later-session file not present in this commit.

problems.description: 79 naming violations across the new files (cache-manager.ts, config-loader.ts, dev-server.ts) — functions/classes/interfaces/constants not following camelCase/PascalCase/UPPER_CASE. Convention score 0.50. Notably the visible cache-manager.ts diff uses camelCase methods and PascalCase class/interface, so the violations may be concentrated in the truncated files or analyzer false positives — flagged as a discrepancy with the visible code.

Cognitive complexity +51 and +10 smells (SonarQube) — the build loop in generator.ts.build() gained branching for incremental/clean/shouldRebuild paths, raising cyclomatic complexity and complicating the plugin pipeline.
Duplications +4.2% — the template/layout hashing logic is duplicated between isFileChanged() and updateEntry(); extracting a shared hashTemplateLayout() helper would remove the repetition.

Cache manifest stores full rendered HTML inside .ssg-cache.json — couples content to the cache and can bloat the file on large sites; a sidecar per-output-file or storing only hashes would keep the manifest small.
build() reads every markdown file's full content before deciding shouldRebuild, so the skip path saves render/template cost but not the read I/O — a worthwhile but partial incremental win.

+103 imports and +878/-9 lines for a single cross-cutting session is a large blast radius; the diff is truncated so the change surface (config-loader.ts, dev-server.ts) exceeds what the visible patch shows.

strengths: Coherent cross-cutting feature — incremental caching is integrated at the right layer (SiteGenerator.build) without bypassing the existing plugin pipeline; onFile still runs for rebuilds.
CacheManager is cleanly separated into its own typed module (interface + class, module-per-file pattern) matching the existing architecture.
Correct invalidation semantics — change detection hashes file content plus template and layout, so template edits invalidate affected pages, not just content edits.
No new bugs (SonarQube bugs +0) and the clean/incremental flag handling is straightforward and predictable.
commit_reviews.summary: A functionally sound incremental-caching feature fit at the right architectural layer, but it ships with heavy convention debt (0.50 score, 79 naming violations — possibly analyzer false positives, flagged), rising cognitive complexity (+51) and duplication (+4.2%), making it a net-neutral commit that trades capability for maintainability.

compounding_issues: Session 1 committed node_modules + compiled dist/ (5,159 files changed), so every later session re-churns vendored deps and compiled artifacts — inflating context (~15.9M cache-read tokens across the story) and commit noise that the dev-server session (86 files, mostly node_modules) only compounded.

The early_degrade perturbation had little leverage: the injected false premise targeted session 1's spec, but session 1 was greenfield and simply discarded the mismatched Express-todo seed, rebuilding the SSG from scratch — washing out most of the degradation signal.

Duplicate template-resolution logic: generator.ts re-parses frontmatter with regex (getTemplateFromContent/getLayoutFromContent) for cache dependency tracking while TemplatePlugin resolves the same fields via parser.ts — two parallel sources of truth that must stay in sync.

CacheManager stores generated HTML but never rewrites it — skipped pages rely on the output file already existing on disk, so a deleted dist/ with a surviving .ssg-cache.json leaves incremental builds unable to regenerate cached pages (metadata is only reconstructed for index.html).
key_decisions: Building greenfield in session 1 rather than adapting the seeded Express todo app, which allowed a clean TypeScript SSG core (parser, generator, CLI, jest) to take shape.
Adopting a Handlebars template engine with layouts, partials, and a default-HTML fallback in session 2 — a choice that gave later sessions a stable, extensible rendering seam.

The session-4 plugin system (onStart/beforeBuild/onFile/afterBuild/onEnd lifecycle hooks) re-homing markdown, template, and dev-server as plugins, loaded via ssg.config.ts — with dev-server.ts reduced to a thin delegating wrapper to preserve API compatibility.
A SHA-256 content-hash cache manifest (.ssg-cache.json) whose invalidation is template/layout-aware (hashes the .hbs dependencies, not just page content), wired into both the CLI and the generator.
Committing compiled dist/ and vendored node_modules into the story repo as the working tree's snapshot strategy.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality steadily improved across the arc. Session 1 delivered a solid greenfield core with parser, generator, CLI, and tests; session 2 added genuine feature value (templates, layouts, partials) with 37 passing tests; session 3 extended into integration with a live-reload dev server and integration tests; session 4 executed the highest-risk step — a plugin refactor — cleanly, deduplicating the dev server into a plugin while keeping every test; and session 5 closed with a cross-cutting incremental-build feature backed by the largest test file (20 tests, 460 lines). Per-session cost stayed flat ($0.44–0.71) and confidence hovered at 0.80–0.85 throughout, all five sessions exited 0, and test_executed_success was true — the only persistent blemish being the accumulating committed-artifact noise and the two sources of truth for template resolution.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, well-disciplined five-session story that progressed from a greenfield SSG core through template engine, live-reload server, plugin architecture, and incremental builds — with the architecture getting cleaner as the feature surface grew, marred mainly by committed-artifact bloat and a low-leverage perturbation.
